email.subject: URGENT: Your account will be locked today
email.body:
Hello valued member,

We recently updated our routine billing checks across member profiles and noticed a pending verification item on your account. If you still use this email address for online payments, please review your details before the end of the day.

URGENT: Your account will be locked today if you do not confirm your recent billing information through our verification portal.

Thank you for banking with us, and we hope you have a smooth week ahead.
email.signature:
PayPai Member Care
Reference #PP-88412
Member Support Desk
email.footer: PayPai Holdings Ltd., 400 Harbor Way, Suite 210.

redFlags.explanation: That domain is a made-up lookalike address rather than an official payment domain. Always check the full sender address before trusting an alert.

redFlags.text: URGENT: Your account will be locked today
redFlags.explanation: Shouting in all caps and threatening an immediate lock is classic panic bait to rush your click. Real services rarely threaten same-day lockouts out of the blue.
A generic 'valued member' greeting instead of your name is common in mass phishing blasts. Scammers send the exact same template to thousands of inboxes.

fieldGuide.howItWorks: Sent in huge waves to thousands of addresses at once using generic greetings and one-size-fits-all panic hooks.
telltaleSigns: Generic greetings like 'Dear customer' or 'Valued user'
Mass-market threats of account closure within 24 hours
Links leading to lookalike domains
fieldGuide.defenseTip: Pause when an email does not know your name and demands instant action; navigate to the service yourself instead of clicking.

email.subject: Autumn Research Stipend — updated form needed
email.body:
Hi there,

I saw your name on the Autumn Research Stipend shortlist for the environmental studies track and wanted to follow up before Friday's roster lock.

We are moving stipend direct-deposit forms to a new single sign-on page this term. Please sign in with your campus credentials so we can keep your grant file active.

Let me know if you have any questions about the timeline.
email.signature:
Maya Lin
Research Coordinator, Fall Cohort
Campus Grants Office
email.footer: Sent regarding Fall Term student research awards.

redFlags.explanation: Even though the message mentions a real-sounding campus program, the sender comes from an external lookalike domain. Double-check that staff emails use your actual institution's domain.

redFlags.text: sign in with your campus credentials
redFlags.explanation: Asking you to enter your campus login details through an emailed form is a big red flag for credential theft. Legitimate coordinators will point you to your regular portal without credential prompts in email.
A button pushing you to a single sign-on page from an unexpected email can lead straight to a fake login screen. Check the real URL carefully before typing a password.

fieldGuide.howItWorks: Researches a specific person, team, or role first so the lure sounds tailored, familiar, and relevant.
telltaleSigns: References to real projects, colleagues, or recent events
Requests that feel slightly 'inside baseball'
Subtle sender domain mismatches
fieldGuide.defenseTip: Verify unusual requests through a second channel—like a quick chat or phone call—using a known contact.

email.subject: Quick favor before my flight — vendor settlement
email.body:
Hi,

I am heading into a flight in twenty minutes and wrapping up a quiet advisory settlement with our external legal counsel before the quarter closes.

Can you handle a quick gift-card purchase for the visiting speakers right now and email me the redemption codes? Keep this off the main thread until the paperwork is filed.

Thanks for jumping on this quickly.
email.signature:
David Vance
Managing Director
NorthStar Ventures

redFlags.explanation: Notice the '.co' domain instead of a standard '.com'—a subtle swap that is easy to miss on a phone screen. Executives impersonated in whaling scams often use close lookalike domains.

redFlags.text: gift-card purchase for the visiting speakers
redFlags.explanation: Asking someone to buy gift cards and send back codes is a classic executive-impersonation trap. Real speaker expenses go through standard reimbursement or vendor channels.

redFlags.text: Keep this off the main thread
redFlags.explanation: Urging secrecy or asking you to keep things off the usual thread is designed to stop you from checking with coworkers. Scammers love quiet requests made right before someone is 'unavailable'.

fieldGuide.howItWorks: Impersonates a senior leader or executive to pressure employees into bypassing normal approval or payment steps.
telltaleSigns: Authority and time pressure ('in a meeting', 'on a flight')
Requests for wire transfers, gift cards, or sensitive files
Hints to keep the request quiet or 'off-thread'
fieldGuide.defenseTip: Treat any urgent money or data request from 'the boss' as suspicious until confirmed via an established process.

email.subject: Re: Updated Syllabus & Lab Schedule (Revised)
email.body:
Hi,

Following up on last week's shared folder thread, here is the revised version of the Syllabus & Lab Schedule with updated room assignments.

Because the earlier attachment had a formatting hiccup, I re-uploaded the clean copy to this replacement link. Please open the revised file to grab the latest dates.

Best,
Samira
email.signature:
CloudBox Document Relay
Shared Workspace Notifications
CloudBox Team
email.footer: Automated file-share notice for your workspace.

redFlags.explanation: This 'sync-share' domain mimics a file-sharing notice rather than coming from your real document service. Always look closely at the domain behind file-update alerts.

redFlags.text: re-uploaded the clean copy to this replacement link
redFlags.explanation: Claiming an earlier file had an error and offering a 'replacement link' is how clone phishers swap in a malicious lure. Treat surprise 'revised copy' links with extra care.
A download button attached to an unexpected 'revised' file notice can steer you to a spoofed page or risky download. Check with the sender before opening replacement links.

fieldGuide.howItWorks: Takes a legitimate or previously sent email, copies its layout and topic, and swaps in a harmful link or attachment.
telltaleSigns: 'Updated' or 'resubmitted' versions of familiar files
Slightly altered sender details or forwarding paths
A new link where you expected a normal document
fieldGuide.defenseTip: Compare against the original message and check the true destination URL before opening 'replacement' files.

email.subject: Overdue balance notice — Statement #PW-4471
email.body:
Hello,

Our accounts receivable log shows an unpaid balance tied to recent poster and lab-binder printing for student clubs.

We have attached a copy of the statement along with the itemized line items for your review. Please check the attached document if you need the breakdown before scheduling payment.

Thanks for your help keeping our ledger tidy.
email.signature:
PrintWave Billing Department
Accounts Receivable
PrintWave Supplies
email.footer: Statement reference #PW-4471. Reply to billing with questions.

redFlags.explanation: A separate '-invoices.net' billing domain is a common cover for fake payment notices. Verify billing emails against known vendor contacts before acting.
Double extensions like '.pdf.exe' hide an executable program behind a document icon. Never run an '.exe' file that pretends to be an invoice or PDF.
Pushing you to click an online statement link on an unexpected invoice notice is a frequent phishing hook. Check your real vendor portal directly instead.

fieldGuide.howItWorks: Uses fake invoices, receipts, or overdue notices to spark worry about money and trick you into opening bad files or links.
telltaleSigns: Unexpected bills or overdue notices for unfamiliar charges
Attachments with tricky or executable file extensions
Payment links on generic or mismatched billing domains
fieldGuide.defenseTip: Never open suspicious attachments or pay through emailed links; check your real account or ask accounting first.

email.subject: Parcel delivery attempt failed — action required
email.body:
Hi customer,

A courier attempted to deliver a package addressed to your location this morning, but could not complete handoff due to an incomplete delivery note.

Your parcel will be returned to the depot unless you confirm a new delivery window and address details right away.

Thank you for using SwiftPost.
email.signature:
SwiftPost Courier Support
Parcel Routing Desk
SwiftPost Logistics
email.footer: Automated delivery status alert from SwiftPost.

redFlags.explanation: A 'redelivery.info' address is a classic sign of a package-tracking phish rather than an official carrier. Always check tracking numbers on the actual carrier's website.

redFlags.text: returned to the depot unless you confirm
redFlags.explanation: Threatening to return a parcel unless you confirm details right away creates artificial urgency. Scammers use missed-delivery scares because people often have packages on the way.
A big 'Reschedule Delivery Now' button in a surprise tracking email often leads to credential or small-fee scams. Look up your order in the store you bought it from instead.

fieldGuide.howItWorks: Dangles a missed delivery, customs fee, or tracking update to get a quick click while you are expecting an order.
telltaleSigns: No tracking number or order details you recognize
Urgent warnings that a package will be returned or held
Shortened or unfamiliar tracking domains
fieldGuide.defenseTip: Skip emailed tracking links and check your order status directly inside the store or carrier app you trust.

email.subject: Unrecognized sign-in attempt on your cloud profile
email.body:
Hello,

Our automated security monitor logged a sign-in attempt from a browser session that looked different from your usual activity.

If this was not you, please sign in immediately to review your active sessions and keep your account protected.

We sent this notice to help keep your workspace safe.
email.signature:
Micro-soft Account Protection
Automated Security Alerts
Micro-soft Cloud Services
email.footer: Security alert sent to protect your cloud account.

redFlags.explanation: This hyphenated 'micro-soft-signon-alert.com' address is a lookalike domain built to trick you. Real security notices come from the service's actual domain.

redFlags.text: sign in immediately to review your active sessions
redFlags.explanation: Pushing you to 'sign in immediately' from an alert email is designed to funnel you onto a fake login page. Open a fresh browser tab to your real account settings instead.
Clicking a sign-in button inside a security email can land you on a credential-harvesting clone. Always navigate to your account page yourself before typing a password.

fieldGuide.howItWorks: Sends you to a cloned login page that looks almost identical to a real sign-in screen to steal your password or code.
telltaleSigns: Lookalike domains with extra words, hyphens, or typos
Security alerts that push you to log in through a link
Login pages missing your password manager autofill
fieldGuide.defenseTip: Bookmark important login pages or type the address yourself—never trust a sign-in link from an email alert.

email.subject: Mailbox sync issue & remote diagnostic check
email.body:
Hi,

Our support queue flagged a recurring sync error between your mail client and cloud storage profile that can cause drafts to stall.

If the issue continues, you can run a quick remote diagnostic session with an agent so we can adjust your local mail settings.

Reach out if you would like help walking through the steps.
email.signature:
Amazun Technical Support
Client Sync & Diagnostics
Amazun Care Team
email.footer: Support ticket follow-up from Amazun Device Care.

redFlags.explanation: Spotting 'amazun' with a 'u' instead of an 'o' catches a subtle lookalike domain. Always check spelling in the sender's address before trusting support messages.

redFlags.text: run a quick remote diagnostic session with an agent
redFlags.explanation: Unsolicited offers to start a remote session on your device are a major warning sign in tech-support scams. Legitimate support teams do not ask you to hand over remote control out of nowhere.
A link inviting you to launch a remote diagnostic tool can install unwanted software or give an attacker access. Contact your official helpdesk directly if you ever need support.

fieldGuide.howItWorks: Pretends to be IT or customer support offering 'urgent fixes,' remote help, or a phone number to call.
telltaleSigns: Unsolicited warnings about 'errors' or 'compromised devices'
Prompts to download tools or grant remote access
Pressure to call an unfamiliar support number
fieldGuide.defenseTip: Never grant remote access or run diagnostic tools from an unsolicited message; contact official support directly.
